The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9131. Fair Warning to Auction Major Yoshitomo Nara Painting for Up to $15 M.

One of Yoshitomo Nara’s largest paintings is also one of his most subtle. Instead of glaring defiantly at the viewer, the child at the center of In the Milky Lake / Thinking One (2011) has her eyes closed and a somewhat serene expression on her face. Her body is half-submerged in a pale pool of water. On November 19, the monumental painting will be offered by Loïc Gouzer’s Fair Warning app with an estimate of $10 million to $15 million.

Measuring 8.5 feet by 6 feet, it’s the largest Nara painting ever to appear at auction. The work has been in private hands for 14 years and will be exhibited in Chelsea at 534 West 22nd Street, which has been designed to resemble a Japanese temple, from November 6–19. Related Articles Jeff Koons Appears to Be the 'Distinguished Collector' Offering $100 M. in Old and Modern Masters at Christie's Fair Warning Heads Underground With Keith Haring Subway Drawing Estimated at Just Under $1 M.

Nara painted the work in 2011, the year the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami devastated northeastern Japan, including the region where he grew up. The disaster left him unable to paint for some time, and when he returned to his studio, something had changed. His familiar cast of angry, sometimes menacing children began to give way to quieter, more introspective figures.

In the Milky Lake / Thinking One was the only major painting he completed that year. It’s since appeared in numerous museum exhibitions, including his 2012 survey in Japan, his 2021 retrospective at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and more recent shows at the Guggenheim Bilbao, Museum Frieder Burda, and Hayward Gallery in London. Nara also included it in his 2015 book Self-Selected Works: Paintings.

The sale will take place alongside the November New York auctions from the Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips. Many of the big-ticket lots being offered are by historical, blue-chip artists whose careers were firmly established in the 20th century, from Kandinsky and Monet to Warhol and Basquiat, as opposed to living contemporary artists. Gouzer, who founded Fair Warning after leaving Christie’s, thinks collectors may be getting ready to look at contemporary art a little differently.

“There was a lot of not very interesting contemporary [art] that was pushed hard and then crashed, deservedly,” Gouzer told ARTnews, referring to the speculative buying that swept through the market between 2021 and 2023.

“The main dogma of the last year and a half, two years, was like, ‘Contemporary is over. It’s only about blue chip,’” he said.

Gouzer isn’t buying it. Nara, he argued, is “as blue chip as it gets for contemporary art,” and his relatively small output sets him apart from some of the younger artists whose markets have taken a beating in recent years. In many cases, collectors paid a premium for work they thought was scarce, only to discover that there was plenty more where it came from.

“Now we’re in a period where people don’t want what their neighbors have,” Gouzer said. “They don’t want something that is like some kind of commodity. Nara is still here and the market is strong, partly because his art is great and also because it’s really rare.”

Nara’s auction record stands at $24.9 million, set at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2019 for Knife Behind Back (2000). His market has cooled somewhat since its peak, although major paintings can still fetch eight figures. A similar work, In the Milky Lake (2012), which shares the present painting’s contemplative imagery, sold for $12.8 million at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2023.

There’s also been a big change in Nara’s gallery representation. In November 2025, David Zwirner announced that it would represent the artist, who had been with Pace Gallery for 14 years. Pace said it would continue working with him. On November 5, Zwirner will open Nara’s first solo exhibition with the gallery, spread across two Chelsea locations, with new paintings, drawings, sculptures, and earlier works chosen by the artist.

Gouzer thinks the gallery change could inject Nara’s market with new interest. “An artist is a musical note, and then the gallery is an instrument,” he said, noting that three monumental Nara sculptures also recently went on view at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C. “So if you change the instrument, you might perceive the note a bit differently.”

Gouzer is confident that Nara’s auction record will eventually fall. He said he wouldn’t be surprised to see a major painting sell for $30 million or even $40 million someday, though he’s not necessarily expecting that to happen this month.

#9130. Foster + Partners unveils replacement for landmark San Siro stadium in Milan

British architecture studio Foster + Partners and US studio Manica have unveiled their design for Generali Stadium, a new football stadium for clubs AC Milan and Inter Milan, set to replace Italy’s iconic San Siro.

Planned to be built alongside the 99-year-old San Siro stadium, which will later be torn down, the 71,500-seat replacement will be defined by a structural facade composed of elongated X-framed concrete supports.

Foster + Partners‘ founder Norman Foster told Dezeen the overarching goal is “to create a new home for two storied football clubs, which captures the unique energy of the city and its distinctive architectural and structural traditions”.

“The Generali Stadium celebrates the enduring connection between the football clubs – FC Internazionale Milano (Inter Milan) and AC Milan – and the city of Milano and will drive this shared heritage into the future,” he explained.

The design reveal follows the sale of the iconic stadium to the two rival football teams, which was approved by Milan’s city council in October 2025. It is being developed by Foster’s firm with the US practice Manica, and the naming rights belong to insurance giant Generali.

AC Milan and Inter Milan will continue to share the existing San Siro venue until the 2032 European Championship, co-hosted by Italy, for which the new stadium is scheduled to be completed. San Siro will then be demolished, according to the BBC.

Generali Stadium’s defining feature is its pre-cast structural facade, which will support the stadium bowl and double-curved roof. This will also frame and naturally ventilate a series of lofty loggia-like spaces on its upper levels, intended to feel open and welcoming.

“The structural facade is the defining architectural concept of the stadium: a holistic and monumental piece of infrastructure rising approximately 60 metres in height, composed of interlocking low-carbon precast concrete segments connected through expressed structural joints,” Foster said.

“It is a celebration of Milanese and Italian engineering tradition, where architecture and structure become one,” Foster explained.

Another distinctive element will be “two curvas” – the curved north and south stands, designed to bring spectators near to the pitch, with opposing fans closely facing each other.

“That relationship of two opposing walls of supporters, each tied to one of the city’s great clubs, is unique to Milan and found in no other stadium in the world,” said Manica founder David Manica.

“The whole seating bowl is built around it,” he told Dezeen. “Rather than starting with an image or an icon, we began with the experience of the fans. The architecture is a result of that guiding principle.”

According to Foster, this design also draws on San Siro’s distinctive structure.

“Its seating bowl is inspired by the San Siro itself, with its distinctive ‘curvas’, but with greater proximity to the pitch,” Foster explained.

“The external shape is driven by the curvas behind the goals. Here, the north and south ends rise on a 37-degree pitch to house 11,700 at each end – north for Internazionale and south for AC Milan.”

The stadium is planned to be all-electric and carbon-neutral in operation, targeting LEED Gold Certification. The roof will incorporate 27,500 square metres of photovoltaic panels, while a “low-carbon precast concrete system” will be utilised to minimise waste and construction time.

The bowl’s geometry will be engineered to “amplify the roar of crowds within the stadium, enhancing the atmosphere during events while significantly reducing acoustic spillover and noise pollution”, Foster said.

“San Siro is famous for its noise, and the best way to honour that legacy was to capture that atmosphere – and amplify it,” added David Manica.

“We treated acoustics as a primary design driver from the very first sketches,” he said. “The result is a stadium where the chanting and singing build on themselves, taking the atmosphere Milanese supporters love and making it even more powerful.”

The project forms part of a wider 281,000-square-metre masterplan that will combine public spaces with green areas and leisure and retail zones.

Designed by architect Ulisse Stacchini, San Siro, otherwise known as Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, was built in 1925. It has been modified several times over its lifetime, but has remained unchanged since the 1990 World Cup.

The possibility of its demolition emerged in 2019, when AC Milan and Inter Milan announced they were exploring plans to build a replacement venue for San Siro.

The clubs later selected a design by architecture studio Populous, called the Cathedral, but the Regional Commission for the Cultural Heritage of Lombardy blocked its development in 2023 because of the existing building’s cultural significance.

Demolition was made possible by the building’s sale, which was approved after an overnight debate that took place for nearly 12 hours.

At the time, mayor Giuseppe Sala suggested the sale would prevent Milan from being left “with the burden of an abandoned arena”, as the two clubs had begun exploring plans to build two separate stadiums on the city’s outskirts.

Reflecting on the project, Foster said the Generali Stadium’s design draws on his “great personal connection with the city”.

“As a student of architecture, I spent many hours walking through and sketching its heroic public spaces – the urban route of the historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II and individual structures such as the Torre Velasca and Pirelli Tower – and studying the pioneering work of Pier Luigi Nervi,” he explained.

“The verticality and rhythm of the Duomo, the civic generosity of the city’s porticos, and the spatial experience of the city’s great public plazas have all been inspirational and inseparable as a background to the design of the Generali Stadium, which will be a new civic monument for Milano.”

Elsewhere, Foster + Partners is also developing its design for Manchester United’s new 100,000-seat stadium in the UK.

The stadium, which is designed with a giant tent-like structure, was described by Foster as “one of the most exciting projects in the world”.

#9129. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#9127. Simon Denny Commissioned by New York Magazine to Create Portraits of ‘New AI Elite’ for Power Issue

For its latest “Power” issue, New York Magazine commissioned Berlin-based artist Simon Denny to illustrate the article “So Few People, So Much Influence,” about 26 AI engineers, founders, and thinkers whose “influence on the AI landscape far outstrips their fame.”

These include people like Logan Graham of Anthropic, whose job is to try and push AI models to do terrifying things like build a bioweapon or enact a cyberattack; Beth Barnes, the founder of METR, a nonprofit that tests AI models before they are released; and Brandan Foddy of Mercor, which trains AI models to take over more jobs and industries. Related Articles Italian Police Used AI to Identify $200 M. Worth of Stolen Art and Antiquities Jewish Digital Cultural Recovery Project Adds AI to Provenance Search Tool

The article, a collaboration with Transformer, a Substack newsletter about the power and politics of AI, includes a footnote explaining that Denny used AI to generate portraits that had the look and feel of VHS tapes. Indeed, each of Denny’s Technologists Portraits, as the series is called, shows a smiling figure with a fake-seeming backdrop depicted in the kind of crackly, oversaturated palette associated with “vintage” media like VHS. The dated, distorted style of the portraits is a powerful contrast to the the power and influence held by this cohort of virtually unknown AI experts.

“With each major paradigm shift in the past 20 years,” Denny explained, “I have tried to map and unpack some of this community’s stories as they narrate our experience of a changing technological world. The distortions of the final compositions are traces of the changes that are coming and the people bringing them about.”

Denny has long explored the intersection between art and technology, and has lately been writing about the topic as well. (In April, he wrote about the aesthetics of defense tech and in October about Polymarket, both for Artforum.) He represented New Zealand in the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015, where his show, “Secret Power,” turned internet servers into vitrines to display leaked documents and visual content about the National Security Agency and an intelligence alliance between the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand known as “Five Eyes.”

More recently, Denny’s piece Output 0971 (2025), from his “Machine Painting” series, was included in the exhibition “Sentient Earth” at Amant. “I’m interested in the stories that are woven by the people making the technology that we end up using,” Denny told ARTnews. “It’s hard to parse what’s mythology and what’s truth when we’re confronting machine learning; it’s really unfamiliar even to those actors who are building it. This is why myth making is so important in the tech space. How does all of this become familiar and normalized?”

#9126. Lighting design a "strategic economic investment" says Signify's Sameer Sodhi

According to business leader of entertainment and Colour Kinetics at lighting brand Signify, Sameer Sodhi, lit-up architecture and public installations can encourage interaction, strengthen local identity and support overall wellbeing.

Sodhi explained that for decades, the value of a building has been measured by appearance, energy performance, return on investment and construction costs. A building’s lighting design is one of the most influential factors but is often overlooked and seen as a “finishing touch”.

He added that well-designed lighting can shape the experience of places, support local economies and strengthen communities.

“The question is no longer whether lighting matters,” Sodhi said. “But whether we can accurately measure the (overlooked) value it creates.”

Sodhi points to a recent study by lighting brand Colour Kinetics that examined four illuminated spaces across the United States and found that lighting generated social, economic, and cultural benefits “well beyond the initial investment”.

“The report assesses lighting through a broader framework that includes community engagement, tourism, economic development, media visibility, partnerships, sustainability and health and wellbeing,” Sodhi explained.

“Rather than viewing lighting as an isolated building system, it recognised it as infrastructure capable of influencing how cities function and how communities connect,” he added.

Sodhi cites the lighting of Daniel Hoan Memorial Bridge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, as an example, which has transformed the infrastructure into a “dynamic visual icon” that reflects the city’s identity and connects residents and visitors to the waterfront.

“The bridge now hosts community and civic events, causes and initiatives and annual festivals, while serving as a canvas for civic celebrations throughout the year,” he said.

According to Sodhi, architectural lighting also creates economic value. For example, the thoughtful lighting design of West Sacramento’s Barns in California has supported the area’s placemaking.

Although the venue was originally conceived as an event and dining venue, the strategic lighting design has helped establish it as the focal point for the surrounding mixed-use district, which includes spaces for hosting concerts, festivals, community activities and sporting events.

Sodhi explained that, because of the building’s lit-up impact, approximately ten residential developments have since been built or are under construction nearby, highlighting the role “quality public spaces” can play in wider regeneration.

“Importantly, the value created extends beyond construction economics,” added Sodhi. “Visitors stay longer, businesses benefit from increased footfall, and the location develops an identity that encourages repeat visits and investment.”

According to Sodhi, lighting can also serve as a form of public communication. For example, Philadelphia City Hall’s lighting is programmed to respond to national celebrations, charitable campaigns and civic events, “transforming a historic landmark into a dynamic expression of the city’s identity”.

“Whether celebrating sporting victories or marking important social causes, the building becomes an active participant in public life rather than simply a backdrop,” added Sodhi.

This also applies to Nashville’s illuminated installation, Loqui, Sodhi explained. The artwork includes words and stories from more than 400 local residents and demonstrates how illuminated public art can amplify local voices and bring a community together.

“Rather than lighting serving the artwork, the lighting becomes integral to the experience itself,” he added.

“These projects suggest that good lighting is no longer simply about visibility. It is about participation.”

Sodhi added that buildings are also assessed by how efficiently they operate, but also how effectively they create meaningful experiences.

“Architectural lighting is uniquely positioned to support that ambition,” he explained. “It can extend the usability of spaces after dark, strengthen local identity, encourage social interaction and help transform ordinary infrastructure into memorable landmarks.”

“When thoughtfully integrated from the earliest stages of design, lighting becomes a strategic investment rather than an aesthetic upgrade,” he added. “Perhaps this is the real measure of good design.”

#9124. Al-Jawad Pike refreshes Aesop store with terracotta-tiled counter evoking ancient Persia

Local studio Al-Jawad Pike has given skincare brand Aesop’s shop in London department store Harrods a revamp, centred on a terracotta-clad counter designed to have “the qualities of a miniature building”.

Aesop has had a counter in Harrods for over a decade. For this revamp, Al-Jawad Pike, which is a long-term collaborator of Aesop’s, aimed to take the design further than a regular beauty-brand counter.

“We were interested in giving the counter the qualities of a miniature building, with suggestions of apertures, openings and floor levels: something designed with the architectural ambition of a building but the care of a cabinet,” Al-Jawad Pike co-founder Jessam Al-Jawad told Dezeen.

“Through carved alcoves we also wanted to recall the architecture of ancient Persia – the highly literate civilisation that developed liquid perfumery.”

The studio drew on Harrods’ easily recognisable red brick facade when designing the central counter, which is clad in terracotta tiles from Italy that were chosen for their ability to hold scents.

“We chose glazed terracotta early on in the process because of its connection to traditional fragrance production, but also because of its strong association with Harrods’ iconic facade,” Al-Jawad explained.

The counter is decorated with an alchemist-style design piece, described by Aesop as an “olfactory sculpture.”

Glass vessels filled with fragrances hang from a copper stand, with copper cones that let visitors experience the different scents.

“The olfactory sculpture is something that Aesop has been independently developing in different forms across a number of their projects,” Al-Jawad Pike explained.

“Our take on this was to create a delicate but organised structure of copper piping and blown glass, through which fragrance-infused air is pushed to scent funnels for customers to interact with.”

The colour palette of the Aesop store complements the monolithic terracotta counter, with brushed copper brought in as a tactile contrast.

“The colour palette was chosen in collaboration with the team at Aesop for its intensity and richness, which we felt resonated with the olfactory experience of fragrance,” Al-Jawad said.

“We paired this with matte, brushed copper because of its connection to fragrance creation and distillation.”

Earlier this year, Aesop launched its first lighting collection at Milan design week. Previous Aesop stores featured on Dezeen include a Barcelona shop by Mesura that won the 2024 Dezeen Award for best interior.

#9123. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#9122. Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam, featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis.

Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music.

Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud.

Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam.

“We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen.

The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach.

Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek, a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport.

Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline.

“We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet.

“We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.”

The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis, who is Cournet’s partner.

Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar.

Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl.

Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency.

Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year.

These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar.

“There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet.

“When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.”

ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam.

The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering.

It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests.

Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme.

“Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet.

“It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.”

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

#9121. misha kahn turns upholstery into painting and marble into fabric at friedman benda

the designer discusses his return to hands-on experimentation, where unexpected materials and processes reshape familiar domestic objects.

Misha Kahn‘s latest exhibition, All Intensive Purposes, brings a radical collection of furniture and sculpture to Friedman Benda, marking ten years of collaboration with the gallery. A sofa resembles a pile of painted shapes, and a marble console seems to sag beneath the drapes of its own fabric-like surface.

The works reveal Kahn’s fascination with material experimentation and the unpredictable ways an idea can develop through the process of making. At the show’s opening, designboom spoke with the artist and designer about the thinking behind these unusual objects and his return to more tactile methods of working.

Throughout the New York gallery, familiar objects take on unexpected qualities. Striped plywood returns to tree-like forms, copper is worked into the appearance of loosely knitted fabric. There’s even a ‘lazy river’ circulating through the space.

For much of his career, Misha Kahn has moved between physical craft and digital experimentation, producing furniture through everything from improvised molds to virtual reality. His earlier work often carried the exaggerated, gravity-defying appearance of objects conceived on a computer screen. This time, he describes a shift toward something more immediate.

‘I think, the past handful of years, I really was doing so much work conceptually, digitally,‘ the artist tells designboom. ‘I think this show was really sort of a studio move.‘ Working partly from his studio in the woods, he describes a spiritual shift toward something ‘really tactile,’ with collage and material experimentation becoming central to the new pieces.

The new upholstered pieces offer one of the clearest examples of Kahn’s current approach. Their rounded forms appear assembled from enormous painted fragments, with irregular cushions that overlap and separate. Kahn explains that the process began with a painted composition, which was subsequently translated into wool by textile studio JG SWITZER. The material was then brought back into the furniture-making process, with patterns used to reconstruct the original painted arrangement across the upholstered surfaces.

‘I’ve never gotten that control over the surface,‘ the artist says, explaining that conventional upholstery typically requires working within the limitations of existing fabrics. The new process allowed him to develop the form and its graphic treatment together.

The construction underneath is equally unconventional. ‘We make the frames in the studio, and they’re welded so that the shapes can really flow,‘ Kahn explains. ‘I find that the most satisfying part is sort of the air between the cushions, because we’re so used to seeing a continuous form.‘ Some of the cushions appear loosely attached, raising questions about which parts can actually be moved, while additional pillow elements extend the composition even further.

Perhaps the exhibition’s most unexpected addition is a miniature lazy river, a winding installation that circulates through the gallery alongside a large video projection. The idea came to Kahn with surprising simplicity. ‘I thought, I don’t know why, I think like the beach,‘ he recalls, laughing. ‘I was like, this show needs a lazy river.‘

The video presents an abstract sequence of actions in which materials are repeatedly manipulated and transformed, eventually producing a kind of juice. ‘I wanted to make this video, like, a really abstract version of what it feels like to make objects,‘ he explains, describing the experience of doing something, taking it apart, and putting it back together over and over again.

Kahn designed a series of plastic bottles to accompany the installation, using the familiar manufacturing process associated with commercial water bottles to produce unusual, doubled forms. The arrangement circles continuously, offering a physical interpretation of the exhibition’s title, All Intensive Purposes, which shifts the familiar expression toward the intensity of making, even when the destination remains uncertain.

Kahn has spent much of his career working somewhere between furniture and sculpture. His pieces maintain a recognizable connection to domestic objects, while their unusual proportions and complex surfaces complicate their intended use. In Throws of Passion, for instance, a substantial marble console is carved to resemble draped fabric, its folds appearing almost weightless despite the solidity of the stone.

Asked whether his practice has recently moved further toward sculpture or functional furniture, Kahn describes both as part of the same imagined environment. ‘I feel like I always just wanted to feel like it’s coming from one world,‘ he says. ‘Objects really communicate an idea because I think you understand them as, like, oh, this is what’s in the house, and this is what goes there.‘

He also acknowledges the freedom that comes with making objects beyond the expectations of furniture. ‘I have really enjoyed making sculpture because it just doesn’t have some of the same kind of requirements,‘ he explains. Still, the distinction appears of limited interest to him. ‘I always feel like it should have both. All of my favorite historical figures did both.‘

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9119. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

It’s daft, sure, but it’s a smart way to tap into the GTA 6 hype without just slapping a logo on a box. Just keep it away from the pool, or your fingers.

#9116. Apple takes "monumental step forward" with first touchscreen MacBook

Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.

Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.

As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.

It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.

“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.

“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”

“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”

Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.

The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.

To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.

Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.

“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”

Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.

“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.

“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”

The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.

Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

#9115. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#9114. hydromechanical forming shapes reflective stainless-steel sculptural objects

jawf explores how hydromechanical forming permanently records internal forces within stainless steel, creating sculptural forms where concavity, convexity, and protected interiority emerge through deformation.

SARAH NAGHAWI edited by christina vergopoulou November 3, 2026 3 min

Presented at Amman Design Week 2026, JAWF is an experimental design collection by Jordanian designer Sarah Naghawi that investigates the plastic deformation of stainless steel through hydromechanical forming. Marking the initial application of this industrial fabrication technique within Jordan’s design sector, the project manipulates sheet metal through the mechanics of positive and negative hydraulic pressure, testing the material limits of steel beyond conventional stamping or cold-rolling methods.

Derived from the Arabic word for an inner chamber or protected cavity, JAWF by designer Sarah Naghawi treats the internal void as an architectural condition defined by displaced matter. The fabrication process introduces hydraulic fluid pressure into welded sheet assemblies, allowing internal forces to inflate, buckle, and displace the metal skin. As the material yields, concave and convex profiles develop as reciprocal structural conditions. The resulting reflective steel volumes permanently retain the deformation traces and stress concentrations applied during the hydraulic expansion, yielding self-supporting enclosures where the deformed metallic skin functions simultaneously as structural shell, envelope, and functional interior.

JAWF is a metal research and design project developed by Jordanian designer Sarah Naghawithe pieces are produced using industrial hydromechanical forming methods applied to sheet steelhighly reflective stainless-steel surfaces mirror surrounding spatial environments and lightingthe design studies the geometry of inflated membranes translated into non-elastic metals

#9113. "Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine"

Tschabalala Self’s sculpture is far from being out of place in Trafalgar Square, writes Priya Khanchandani.

Who belongs in public space? How should public art represent who we are? And who deserves to be celebrated, cast in bronze and placed on a pedestal? These are some of the questions that Tschabalala Self’s commission for the Fourth Plinth, Lady in Blue, has raised in recent months, since it was unveiled in September.

I was there that cloudy morning in Trafalgar Square – a space I’d always crossed, probably like most Londoners, without thinking much about what it symbolises. When the black cloth was pulled away, we saw the figure of a Black woman caught mid-stride, one leg pushing through the fabric of her bright blue dress.

Like most of the admirals and generals monumentalised around her, she is cast in bronze. But unlike them she isn’t posed in command, she’s on her way somewhere. Her head, hair piled high, looks straight out into the city towards Whitehall, her left arm and fingers outstretched, moving with intention.

My Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist

I couldn’t help but feel satisfaction that a sculpture of a Black woman was there, taking up space in the city, on what is probably the most visible public plinth in Britain, and assumed this sentiment would be widely shared. It turns out I was wrong; my Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist and often suggesting the sculpture doesn’t fit its context.

I feel the need, therefore, to address the notion of what and who belongs in public space, and particularly in a space like Trafalgar Square.

Before Trafalgar Square existed, the site was used for the royal stables that served Whitehall Palace. Designed in 1840 by Charles Barry, the square was conceived as a stage for Britain’s image of itself, articulated through the grandeur of neoclassicism, and statues were central to its story. If you linger, you’ll spot George IV in Roman robes, sitting valiantly astride his horse. The generals Henry Havelock and Charles James Napier, whose reputations were made in the violent consolidation of British rule in India (the latter for the conquest of Sindh, where all four of my grandparents happen to be from) stand on two further plinths.

Admiral Horatio Nelson himself, the Royal Navy officer whose victory at the Battle of Trafalgar gave the square its name, overlooks them from 50 metres high atop a granite Corinthian column, guarded by four bronze lions. This composition represents a particular vision of 19th-century imperial power, reflected in the monuments and civic spaces rolled out across the Empire.

The square might be beautiful, and a fitting monument to its time, but it is also a living, breathing entity formed not only through its monuments and buildings, but also through the way it has been used.

Its function and meaning as a civic space keep being shaped by the people who have held festivals, memorials, gatherings here – or even simply walked through it on their daily commute. After it was built, Trafalgar Square quickly became a place for public assembly. From Bloody Sunday to the suffragettes to Black Lives Matter and the Palestine Coalition, it has a long tradition as a space of protest.

The square has been redesigned over and over, most significantly by Foster + Partners and Atkins in a 2003 scheme that closed the road along its northern edge, adding a terrace and turning what was essentially a traffic island into a pedestrianised space.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual

Lady in Blue is in dialogue with this context. She echoes the other figures here through her medium, bronze. And yet while the other figures are rooted to their respective plinths, she looks frozen in motion, echoing the movement of the people in the square below rather than the stillness of statues. The vivid blue of the figure’s dress – evoking lapis lazuli, the stone that has been ground into pigment since antiquity – is far from an attack on the Western canon, but rather in conscious conversation with it.

Once intended for an equestrian statue of William IV, the Fourth Plinth stood empty for more than 150 years before it became a space for contemporary sculpture in 1998. Unoccupied, it was always suggestive of a history waiting to be told or – given that the sculptures around it were all commemorating a contemporary moment – a future moment waiting to be solidified in bronze.

The absence of a statue suggested the question of who belongs on a pedestal was always open. Its dedication to contemporary art has allowed for redefinition and offered a chance to bring a quite spectacular historic space, a space of democracy, protest and celebration, into sync with the present.

The Fourth Plinth has become a space where identities are made visible and histories challenged, from Marc Quinn’s powerful Alison Lapper Pregnant, to Yinka Shonibare’s sculpture of Nelson’s own ship in a bottle. Works like these have also, at times, provoked arguments about how the square should be used, and yet each of them has become a part of its changing meaning.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual – and yet, this year’s sculpture underscores why it exists and why it’s so necessary right now.

In 2026, when a Black woman crossing this space is one of the most ordinary sights imaginable, Self’s statue validates her as worthy of belonging, not just in the city but here, in a culturally and politically charged public space dominated by white men sculpted by other white men.

Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for

That elevating such a woman into the visual language of the monument should provoke rage is telling, especially when all the figure has done is walk. Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for.

Self has said her work is meant to speak to human experience beyond racial identity. She has described the sculpture as depicting “everywoman”, implying that an ordinary person merits acknowledgement.

In other words, she hasn’t put it into the world simply as a statement about race – though its reception shows how readily the presence of a Black woman in this setting becomes about who is allowed to stand for the universal.

It’s as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine. At such a fractured time, I can’t help but feel relieved she is there, elbowing her way through the noise, making room for all of us.

Priya Khanchandani is a writer and curator specialising in contemporary design and visual culture. She was formerly head of curatorial at the Design Museum, where she curated the exhibition The Offbeat Sari and an accompanying book. She was also previously editor-in-chief of Icon, while her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Frieze, The Guardian and The World of Interiors, as well as numerous books.

#9112. Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade

In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.

Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.

It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.

The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.

Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.

Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.

“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.

“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.

Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.

“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.

“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”

On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.

The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.

“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”

The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.

“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”

More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.
